cemc-hypatia-2003-01a.title: Two expressions for the number of tiles
cemc-hypatia-2003-01a.body:
Let $N$ be the number of tiles. Then $N = n^2 + 92$ and $N = (n + 2)^2 - 100$.

Equating: $n^2 + 92 = n^2 + 4n + 4 - 100$, so $4n = 188$ and $n = 47$.

Then $N = 47^2 + 92 = 2209 + 92 = 2301$.

**Answer: 2301 tiles**

cemc-hypatia-2003-01a.title: Think about the border
cemc-hypatia-2003-01a.body:
Going from an $n \times n$ square to an $(n+2) \times (n+2)$ square needs $(n+2)^2 - n^2 = 4n + 4$ more tiles. Quentin has $92$ spare tiles and would need $100$ more, so $4n + 4 = 192$, $n = 47$. He has $47^2 + 92 = 2301$ tiles.

**Answer: 2301 tiles**

cemc-hypatia-2003-01b.title: Set up a cubic equation
cemc-hypatia-2003-01b.body:
Quentin has $8^3 - 24 = 488$ blocks. If Rufus' cube has edge $r$, then
$$r^3 + 488 = (r + 2)^3 = r^3 + 6r^2 + 12r + 8,$$
so $6r^2 + 12r - 480 = 0$, i.e. $r^2 + 2r - 80 = 0$, $(r + 10)(r - 8) = 0$. Since $r > 0$, $r = 8$, and the total is $(8 + 2)^3 = 1000$.

**Answer: 1000 blocks**

cemc-hypatia-2003-01b.title: Difference of consecutive-ish cubes
cemc-hypatia-2003-01b.body:
We need two cubes $r^3$ and $(r+2)^3$ that differ by $488$. Differences for small $r$: $r = 6$: $512 - 216 = 296$; $r = 7$: $729 - 343 = 386$; $r = 8$: $1000 - 512 = 488$ ✓. The difference $6r^2 + 12r + 8$ increases with $r$, so $r = 8$ is the only solution and there are $10^3 = 1000$ blocks.

**Answer: 1000 blocks**

cemc-hypatia-2003-02a.title: Mirror Xavier
cemc-hypatia-2003-02a.body:
Yolanda's strategy: whenever Xavier removes some coins from one pile, she removes the same number from the other pile.

After each of Yolanda's turns the two piles are equal. Xavier can never take the last coin, because when it is his turn the two piles are equal; if one is empty both are, and the game is already over. Whenever he empties a pile, the other pile is non-empty and Yolanda empties it, taking the last coin. Since coins keep being removed, the game ends, and it must end with Yolanda's move. ∎

cemc-hypatia-2003-02a.title: Check every case
cemc-hypatia-2003-02a.body:
Xavier's possible first moves (from $3,3$) and Yolanda's replies:
- to $0,3$: Yolanda takes all $3$ and wins.
- to $1,3$: Yolanda moves to $1,1$; Xavier must go to $1,0$; Yolanda wins.
- to $2,3$: Yolanda moves to $2,2$; Xavier goes to $0,2$ (Yolanda takes $2$ and wins) or $1,2$ (Yolanda moves to $1,1$ and wins as above).

In every case Yolanda wins. ∎

cemc-hypatia-2003-02b.title: Make two equal piles
cemc-hypatia-2003-02b.body:
From part (a): if it is Xavier's turn with two equal piles (and no other coins), Yolanda wins by copying his moves.

So Yolanda only needs to reach such a position after her first move. Xavier's possible first moves from $1, 2, 3$, with Yolanda's reply:

| Xavier leaves | Yolanda leaves |
|---|---|
| $0, 2, 3$ | $0, 2, 2$ |
| $1, 1, 3$ | $1, 1, 0$ |
| $1, 0, 3$ | $1, 0, 1$ |
| $1, 2, 2$ | $0, 2, 2$ |
| $1, 2, 1$ | $1, 0, 1$ |
| $1, 2, 0$ | $1, 1, 0$ |

In every case she leaves two equal piles and an empty pile, then wins with the copying strategy. ∎

cemc-hypatia-2003-02b.title: Binary (Nim) view
cemc-hypatia-2003-02b.body: Write the pile sizes in binary: $1 = 01$, $2 = 10$, $3 = 11$. In each binary place there is an even number of $1$s (the "Nim-sum" is $0$). Any move changes exactly one pile and so makes some place odd; and from any position where some place is odd, the next player can restore all places to even. The final position (no coins) has all places even. So the player who always hands over an "all even" position — here Yolanda, since the start is already all even — takes the last coin. Concretely, her replies are exactly those in the table of the first solution. ∎

cemc-hypatia-2003-03.title: Radii as functions of h
cemc-hypatia-2003-03.body:
Let the plane be at height $h$ ($0 \le h \le 10$).

**Cone.** By similar triangles (vertex at height $10$, base radius $5$), the radius at height $h$ is $r_1 = \frac{5}{10}(10 - h) = \frac{10 - h}{2}$.

**Sphere.** The centre is at height $5$. The cross-section at height $h$ is at distance $|h - 5|$ from the centre, so by Pythagoras $r_2^2 = 5^2 - (h-5)^2 = 10h - h^2$.

Equal areas means $r_1^2 = r_2^2$:
$$\frac{(10-h)^2}{4} = 10h - h^2 \implies 100 - 20h + h^2 = 40h - 4h^2 \implies h^2 - 12h + 20 = 0,$$
so $(h - 2)(h - 10) = 0$. At $h = 10$ the plane only touches the cone's vertex and the top of the sphere (both "circles" are single points), so the genuine answer is $h = 2$.

**Answer: 2 cm** (the official solution also lists the degenerate $h = 10$ cm)

cemc-hypatia-2003-03.title: Check h = 2
cemc-hypatia-2003-03.body:
At $h = 2$: the cone's radius is $\frac{10-2}{2} = 4$; the sphere's cross-section is $3$ below the centre, so its radius is $\sqrt{25 - 9} = 4$. Both circles have radius $4$ cm, area $16\pi$. ✓ The quadratic $h^2 - 12h + 20$ has only the other root $h = 10$ (the tangent/vertex plane).

**Answer: 2 cm**

cemc-hypatia-2003-04a.title: One triangle
cemc-hypatia-2003-04a.body:
From $P(2, -6)$, below the square and between $x = 1$ and $x = 5$, only $A$ and $B$ are visible, so the visible area is the area of $\triangle ABP$.

Its base $AB = 4$ lies on $y = 4$; the height is the vertical distance from $P$ to that line, $4 - (-6) = 10$. Area $= \frac12 \cdot 4 \cdot 10 = 20$. ∎

cemc-hypatia-2003-04b.title: Two triangles
cemc-hypatia-2003-04b.body:
From $Q(11, 0)$ (to the right of and below the square) the vertices $A$, $B$, $C$ are visible, and the visible area is $\triangle QBC + \triangle QBA$.

- $\triangle QBC$: base $BC = 4$ on $x = 5$, height $11 - 5 = 6$, area $12$.
- $\triangle QBA$: base $BA = 4$ on $y = 4$, height $4 - 0 = 4$, area $8$.

Total: $12 + 8 = 20$. ∎

cemc-hypatia-2003-04b.title: Shoelace formula
cemc-hypatia-2003-04b.body:
The two triangles form quadrilateral $Q\,C\,B\,A$. By the shoelace formula with $A(1,4)$, $B(5,4)$, $C(5,8)$, $Q(11,0)$:
$$\tfrac12\left|(1\cdot4-5\cdot4)+(5\cdot8-5\cdot4)+(5\cdot0-11\cdot8)+(11\cdot4-1\cdot0)\right| = \tfrac12|-16+20-88+44| = 20. \;∎$$

cemc-hypatia-2003-04c.title: Region by region
cemc-hypatia-2003-04c.body:
**Opposite a side.** If $P$ is directly below the square ($1 \le x \le 5$), the visible area is one triangle with base $4$, so its height must be $10$: $P$ is on the segment from $(1,-6)$ to $(5,-6)$, length $4$. By symmetry there are four such segments (below, above, left, right), each of length $4$.

**Opposite a corner.** If $x \ge 5$ and $y \le 4$, the visible area is $\frac12 \cdot 4(x - 5) + \frac12 \cdot 4 (4 - y) = 2(x - 5) + 2(4 - y)$. Setting this to $20$: $x - y = 11$. In this region that is the segment from $(5, -6)$ to $(15, 4)$ (which contains $Q(11,0)$), of length $\sqrt{10^2 + 10^2} = 10\sqrt2$. It joins the ends of the "below" and "right" segments. By symmetry there are four such segments.

So the 20/20 set is an octagon with four sides of length $4$ and four of length $10\sqrt2$:
$$\text{perimeter} = 16 + 40\sqrt2.$$

**Answer: $16 + 40\sqrt{2}$**

cemc-hypatia-2003-04c.title: Find the vertices
cemc-hypatia-2003-04c.body:
The octagon's vertices are the points $10$ units from the square straight out from each corner along the sides' directions: $(1,-6), (5,-6), (15,4), (15,8), (5,18), (1,18), (-9,8), (-9,4)$. (Each one is the end of a "height 10" segment.) The side lengths alternate: $(1,-6)\to(5,-6)$ is $4$; $(5,-6)\to(15,4)$ is $10\sqrt2$; and so on around. Total $4 \cdot 4 + 4 \cdot 10\sqrt2 = 16 + 40\sqrt2$.

**Answer: $16 + 40\sqrt{2}$**
